title: Cell Phone Policies That Actually Work, Rated
author: Ashlee
summary: Ashlee rates the school cell phone policies districts are using, from bell-to-bell bans with strict storage down to honor-system no-show rules. Drawing on Angela Duckworth's Phones in Focus survey of more than 20,000 educators, she argues that stricter policies produce happier teachers and fewer phones out, and that the policy matters more than the product. Yondr pouches get a middling rating because of cost, durability and workarounds, while free or cheap options such as classroom caddies and off-and-away rules score well provided administrators enforce them consistently. The piece closes with its organising claim: only physical separation between student and device works, and the real question is whether a school will enforce it. It is a ratings-format piece with some promotional-looking numbers, but the school-policy comparison is the whole subject.
points: Bell-to-bell bans with physical storage outperform every other approach, and the policy matters more than which storage product is used.
Yondr pouches shift enforcement off teachers but cost $25-$30 per student plus replacements, while students reverse-engineer them, so free alternatives look comparable.
Classroom phone caddies give a five-second visual compliance check for under $25 without district approval.
Off-and-away policies are free but collapse without consistent, public administrative backing, and honor-system no-show policies underperform everything else.
Physical distance from the device, not rules or reminders, is the common thread in every approach that works.
quotes: Angela Duckworth’s Phones in Focus study surveyed more than 20,000 educators and found two consistent patterns: the stricter the policy, the happier the teacher, and the less likely students are to have phones out when they shouldn’t. Bell-to-bell bans with physical storage, whether pouches, lockers, or caddies, outperform every other approach.

The verdict: Yondr works better than no policy. It works worse than districts expect given what it costs. The physical infrastructure does shift enforcement off individual teachers, which matters. But $30 per student for a product kids reverse-engineer in week two is a hard sell when free alternatives produce comparable outcomes.
This is the classroom-level solution that actually works without requiring a district-wide infrastructure overhaul.

The verdict: the right choice for schools that can’t afford pouches and have strong administrative backing. It doesn’t work on teacher goodwill alone. It works on school-wide consistency. If your admin won’t back you up, this policy will fall apart by October.

The Phones in Focus data is direct: no-show policies perform worse than every other approach. The phone is still there. Still buzzing. Still a centimeter from their hand. A 2025 survey from Common Sense Media found 97% of students use their phones during the school day for a median of 43 minutes. No-show policies don’t move that number.

The approaches that actually work share one thing: physical separation. Not rules about phones. Not reminders. Not consequences on paper. Actual distance between the student and the device for a sustained period. Every study, every teacher survey, every district that has seen real results points to the same conclusion: if the phone is in the room, it is still in the conversation.

Because banning phones and actually removing phones are two completely different things. We rated every approach districts are using right now, from the $7 million pouch systems to the free policy you can implement Monday morning.
